name: Cambridge Analytica

summary.text: Cambridge Analytica was a political data and consulting company founded in 2013 as a subsidiary of SCL Group. In December 2019 the U.S. Federal Trade Commission issued an opinion and final order finding that the company had violated Section 5 of the FTC Act by using deceptive practices to obtain personal information from tens of millions of Facebook users, via an app built by Aleksandr Kogan, for voter profiling and targeting, and by making false claims about its participation in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield. The UK Information Commissioner's Office fined Facebook £500,000 in 2018 for failing to protect users' data from the app, and SCL Elections was fined £15,000 after pleading guilty to failing to comply with an ICO enforcement notice. Cambridge Analytica and SCL Group began insolvency proceedings in the UK and US in May 2018.

facts.claim: On December 6, 2019, the FTC issued an opinion finding that Cambridge Analytica violated Section 5 of the FTC Act by using deceptive practices to obtain personal information from tens of millions of Facebook users for voter profiling and targeting, and by making false or deceptive claims about its participation in and compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
facts.quote: The Opinion found that the company used deceptive practices to obtain personal information from tens of millions of Facebook users for voter profiling and targeting.

facts.claim: The FTC's administrative complaint alleged that users of an app built by Aleksandr Kogan were told it would not collect their names or other identifiable information, while the app in fact collected Facebook User IDs that tie people to their profiles.
facts.quote: Users were allegedly told the app would not collect their names or other identifiable information. In practice, the app collected Facebook User IDs, which tie people to their profiles.

facts.claim: Cambridge Analytica did not file an answer to the FTC complaint, which under FTC rules waived its right to contest the charges; the Commission entered a final order requiring the company to delete the Facebook data it improperly obtained along with associated work product and to meet continuing Privacy Shield obligations.
facts.quote: The injunction requires, among other things, that the company delete the Facebook data it improperly obtained, along with all associated work product.

facts.claim: In October 2018 the UK Information Commissioner's Office fined Facebook £500,000, the maximum under the Data Protection Act 1998, finding that Facebook failed to keep users' personal information secure by failing to perform suitable checks on third-party apps and developers, allowing Aleksandr Kogan's app "This is your digital life," developed on behalf of Cambridge Analytica, to scrape data of up to 87 million users.
facts.quote: The ICO concluded that Facebook had failed to keep the personal information of its users secure by failing to perform suitable checks on the third-party apps and developers using its platform.

facts.claim: In October 2019 Facebook agreed to pay the ICO's £500,000 fine after more than a year of appeals, without admitting liability.
facts.quote: Facebook agreed to pay the fine after more than a year of litigation and back-and-forth appeals between the regulator and the tech giant. As part of the agreement, Facebook made no admission of liability.

facts.claim: The ICO's report to Parliament of 6 November 2018 described its investigation into data analytics in political campaigns, launched in May 2017, as the most complex data protection investigation it had conducted; it recommended a statutory code of practice for the use of personal information in political campaigns and stated that Cambridge Analytica was a trading name of SCL Elections Ltd.

openQuestions: The Mercer and Bannon figures are from DeSmog's profile; confirm against the underlying New York Times and Guardian reporting.
Exact date of the SCL Elections guilty plea (reported January 2019) should be confirmed from the ICO's statement.
The ICO's own penalty notice and final report to Parliament were not among the sources returned; cite them directly if available.

The Mueller report's references to Cambridge Analytica were not read from the report itself; press accounts say investigators' interest related to Alexander Nix's outreach to WikiLeaks. Check the report (justice.gov/archives/sco) before recording any claim.

NPR names the pro-Trump super PAC that paid $5.7 million as 'Stop Crooked Hillary PAC'; the Campaign Legal Center identifies Make America Number 1 as the 'Defeat Crooked Hillary' super PAC. Confirm which committee name the FEC records use.
Whether the FEC acted on MUR 7147 or on the Bolton super PAC complaint was not found.

Site claim test (Manufacturing Consent): 'harvested data from up to 87 million Facebook users' is supported by Facebook's own 4 April 2018 figure ('up to 87 million', an upper estimate); 'the FTC fined Facebook $5 billion' is supported by the FTC's 24 July 2019 announcement, though the $5 billion was a settlement penalty for violating a 2012 FTC order in which Facebook did not admit wrongdoing, rather than a litigated fine.
The FTC press release is cited here from the ICPEN mirror; the owner may wish to replace it with the ftc.gov page of the same title.

Nigeria 2015: the hacking claims rest on Wylie's testimony and anonymous sources reported by the Guardian; no official finding that hacking occurred was located. Does any regulator's record address it?
Lukoil pitch date: Observer-based reporting places the presentation in 2014; Senator Feinstein's May 2018 statement refers to white papers and briefings to Lukoil in 2016. Which is correct?
